title: Look again
hook: look at the sky again and again: do you see any flaw (67:3–4)

segments.voice: Yesterday: ahsanu 'amalan, named in that order, and your line, best in deed. Did one thing get done best instead of most? Al-Mulk keeps going, and now it points up. Day six hundred thirty-eight.

When did you last look at the sky on purpose? Not to check the weather on the way to the car. Not a photo of a sunset for someone else. Just looked, and kept looking, from a bus window or a back step or a parking lot. The third verse of al-Mulk doesn't describe the sky and move on. It gives the reader an assignment. Look. Then look again. Then once more. Go ahead and try to find a flaw.

Verse three says Allah created seven heavens, one above another, tibaqan, in layers. Then, in Pickthall's translation: "Thou (Muhammad) canst see no fault in the Beneficent One's creation; then look again: Canst thou see any rifts?" Two words to notice. Fault translates tafawut: a mismatch, things that don't fit together, a seam that doesn't line up. Rifts translates futur: cracks, splits, gaps. So the question is: anywhere up there, does it fall apart? And then verse four raises the stakes. Look again, twice more, karratayn, and your sight will come back to you worn out and dim, having found nothing. It's a challenge, and it's a dare the verse expects you to lose. You can look until your eyes ache. Notice what the verse is not saying. It doesn't ask you to stop looking because the answer is already known. It asks you to keep looking, again and again, because the looking is the point. The Qur'an asks this kind of question elsewhere too: do they not see, do they not reflect, do they not consider. Some Muslim readers have taken these verses as an invitation to study the natural world, the night sky included. Astronomers in Muslim lands tracked the stars, partly to fix prayer times and the direction of Mecca. But you don't need an observatory for this verse. You need a window, or a patch of sky above a parking lot, and the patience to look a second time, when your eyes start to see what they skipped the first time.

The practice: look up, twice. If you can see the sky, a window is fine, look at it now. If you can't, close your eyes and picture the last sky you saw. First look: take it in, the whole thing, color, light, any cloud. Then close your eyes for a breath. Second look: slower. Find one thing you missed. An edge of cloud, a bird, a contrail, the way the blue changes near the ground. Stay with that one thing. The bell holds the time.
Look again. In 67:3–4 the Qur'an invites the reader to look at the sky, then again and again, for any mismatch or crack, and come back worn out. Today's word.
Your line: the looking is the point. Once today, outside, stop and look up for longer than feels normal. Then look a second time, and find what the first look missed. Day six hundred thirty-eight.

howItsDone: Muslims read 67:3–4, often nightly as part of al-Mulk, as an invitation to contemplate creation (tafakkur); astronomers in Muslim lands studied the sky, partly to set prayer times and the direction of Mecca.

fork.setup: you've looked at the sky once for any crack or flaw. what does verse four tell you to do next?
fork.reveal: look again, twice more. your sight comes back worn out and dim, having found no rift.

original.note: Arabic, 67:3: so turn your sight back, look again.

trapdoor: what you thought: the sky is pretty.
what it means: the verse dares you to look again and again for a flaw in creation, and you'll find none.
what a scholar hears: tafawut is mismatch, futur is cracks, and karratayn, twice, is read by commentators as 'again and again'.
